row.Text: I bet it originated in the Xerox PARC/Smalltalk community because they pioneered both GUIs, IDEs, and WYSIWYG editing. They definitely used interactive development environments where the running program could be inspected and modified on the fly. But I don't have a good reference for that at hand. Many Xerox PARC ideas on GUIs were popularized by Apple with its Lisa and Macintosh products, and Objective-C merged high-level Smalltalk OOP features with the more efficient C language.
Indeed, it was probably Smalltalk's IDE. Here a demo of the Smalltalk-80 verdion from the records of a conference held in 1983: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=JLPiMl8XUKU

Related: [History of the graphical user interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_graphical_user_interface) - the article does not contain much about GUI designers, but before asking about the latter, one should look at the availability timeline of GUIs themselves.
I also found [this interesting article](https://retool.com/visual-basic) about the history of Visual Basic.

@amon: Not sure. I have the feeling a GUI designer tool would have violated Alan Kay's sense of aesthetics. He probably would have argued that, if you need a tool to help you program, your language is too hard and the correct way to fix it would be to make a better language instead of creating a crutch that papers over the language's deficiencies. I think their idea was that if you model the domain correctly, then objects should "just know" how to display themselves, similar to what is now called *Naked Objects*. I.e., the GUI would be a naturally emerging property of the Domain Model.

@JörgWMittag: I don't know about Alan Kay's mindset, but my sense of aesthetics tells me that for creating graphical parts of a program using a graphical tool feels much more natural than using a textual description. And I am sure I am not alone with that opinion.

@DocBrown, worth remembering that the VB forms designer produced a scripted version somewhat similar to VB itself - so there was never an absence of script. In DotNet, this was carried through to its conclusion, and the forms designer produces bona fine VB.NET/C# code. One of the most beneficial aspects of Microsoft software is that almost anything achievable through the GUI has either a scripted representation, or a scriptable alternative for automation.

@Steve: mostly true, still my comment adresses the idea of *" a GUI as a naturally emerging property of the Domain Model"* - which I think is, honestly, overidealistic nonsense. The representation you are talking of are mos easily and naturally edited with a graphical designer, even when they are technically textual, which sometimes allows some direct tweaks with a text editor - but that is not what I am talking of.
Not sure if [ResEdit](https://apple.fandom.com/wiki/ResEdit) fits your definition but it existed long before VB.

@ShyamalParikh: the issue of having "a lot of users" is usually not handled at the "permission per page" part of the architecture. It is mitigated by the option of having user groups which get assigned the same permissions by default. Otherwise, even the manual administrative work of giving each user the right permissons becomes unwieldy.

I'm team "store IDs as properties". It seems to be the only solution that doesn't have other severe problems. You correctly note potential consistency issues, but you're usually not trying to sabotage yourself. Depending on language there might be tricks to improve safety, e.g. using a custom type for IDs that can only be constructed within the entity's owner (like a database interface), and cannot be constructed within client code /business logic. Regarding reverse lookups, note that an object's *address* can often be used as a key.

*"Another intuitive solution would be to store IDs as properties in objects, but then I get no guarantee that they match the actual index of an element in said data structure. "* - sorry, but I have trouble to understand this. Which data structure you are talking of at that point, and why should an ID (which might be a GUID, no number) "match some index" here? An object with a unique, immutable string ID as a property should do the trick, I don't understand which issues you see with that approach.

I've seen the 2 approach, the 1st is elegant but require a mutable ID in your object: the ORM works like this, the 2nd is more robust but require an envelop, it's what is used in elasticsearch. maybe theses 2 examples will help you see in which case you are.

What makes the objects unhashable, mutability? What issues are you facing with assigning a key to each object and using that as a key in a dictionary? Using complex objects as keys in a dictionary tends to have limited usefulness because you need to create an equivalent object in order to find the mapping.

@DocBrown The data structure I talked about was ID → object. The problem I noted with ID as property is that I get no guarantee from the language that at some point I wouldn't produce 2 objects with the same ID, the same way I'd be prevented to add second object under a key in a dictionary.

@JimmyJames Assigning a key to each object and storing them in a dictionary is not a problem. What I had conceptual troubles with is doing reverse search, having in mind the risk when ID is stored as a property (see comment above).

@amon Thank you. Like you mentioned, the availability of these solutions could differ between languages, but the first one seems very elegant, while the second might be more versatile and easier to implement. I will remember both.

*"that I get no guarantee from the language that at some point I wouldn't produce 2 objects with the same ID,"* - sorry, but what has this to do with the programming language? I think this is a property of the generation process. For example, using GUIDs as IDs will guarantee that the risk of getting an ID collision is so low you can assume no duplicate IDs for all practical purposes.

@pdem It's interesting to hear that the envelope solution is actually used in practice. Do you know if the elements find themselves each time when the envelope is created, or is this information stored elsewhere? I suppose it's not the overhead caused by the envelope's size that's problematic.
@DocBrown Fair point.

@Etua To add to what DocBrown mentioned, if you are using random (version 4) [UUIDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier), the chance of collisions is low. If you use a MAC-address-based UUIID (version 1 or 2) you are guaranteed to never have a collision.

Perhaps a more useful viewpoint is: conceptually, every account/session already has an empty cart. You're just deferring storage until there's at least one item. The condition "cart storage must exist before an item can be added" sounds like an internal implementation detail, not like something that should be exposed via public APIs. Arguably, this is because of the SRP: maintaining its own data integrity must be the service's responsibility. It would violate SRP if clients are responsible for that. Possible exception: cart creation has business-level consequences, e.g. a paid subscription.

`the "add to cart" operation also implicitly creates a cart, which violates the single responsibility principle.` -- That's not true at all. The SRP is informed by *variations* in your functional requirements; all you have here is one requirement (The requirement being that a cart must always exist before you can add something to it). Such a requirement cannot vary in any way; i.e. it is not possible to add something to a cart that doesn't exist, therefore you have no variations, therefore the creation of the cart and add/remove operations all fall under the same responsibility.

Eric Evans' definition only focuses on the difference between entities and *value objects*. It doesn't imply anything else. Entities are something that conceptually has some sort of a persistent ID (that may outlive a session in your application). If you have two instances, you determine equality by that ID, and then resolve any conflicts in terms of other properties if they don't match. Value objects are things where you consider two instances to be the same only if all of their properties are equal (no ID needed), and you don't care which instance (of the two) you're working with. 1/2

Value objects are things like ints, or (x, y) coordinates, or dates, or statuses - any type (simple or composite) where the exact value is the primary thing that determines equality (identity). Now, whether or not you need to track some state of an entity during its lifecycle is a completely separate issue and depends on what your entity represents. If there are stages in its lifecycle that you want to track, then you add a property to track that (note that such a property is likely to be a value object). 2/2
